title: Should You Quit Your Teaching Job? (Or: It's October Again)
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: In this reflective piece written for the difficult October stretch of the school year, Dave Stuart Jr. addresses teachers who are wondering whether to quit. His central move is counterintuitive: rather than urging teachers to simply push through, he argues they should first give themselves honest permission to consider quitting, on the grounds that all work is dignified and that teachers have transferable skills. Only once quitting is genuinely back on the table, he argues, does staying become a real choice rather than a trap. He then offers a one-month experiment for teachers in a hard season: practice satisficing, set and protect strict working hours, and experiment with strategies from his book The Will to Learn to rebuild student motivation. The piece closes by asking teachers to use that month to take an honest look at their circumstances rather than deciding out of exhaustion.
points: Stuart argues teachers should deliberately "not rule quitting out" first, because treating it as a genuine option removes the trapped feeling that makes hard seasons unbearable.
He frames satisficing as an essential teaching skill: doing most tasks to a merely satisfactory level so that lesson planning, curriculum understanding, and student relationships get maximal effort.
He recommends a strict, shared, accountability-backed work schedule as the practical enforcement mechanism for satisficing, since without hard stop times teachers can't force themselves to triage.

He roots the "give it a month" advice in Will to Learn strategies for rebuilding student motivation, on the theory that a season's despair is often driven by demotivated students rather than the job itself.
quotes: All of us have skills and aptitudes that would allow us to flourish in other jobs. Though a job transition from education into something else may be challenging, it wouldn't be impossible for any of us.

Provided you don't job-switch into slinging meth or running a brothel, I'd have a hard time arguing that the work you shift into isn't a good and worthy endeavor. Whether you become a plumber or a mechanic or a marketer or an entrepreneur, it's all good work.

I think that when quitting is viewed as a non-option, that's when a hard season in teaching can become truly insufferable. That said, teaching is beautiful and noble work, and I hope that you'll stay.

The gist is this: there are too many tasks in teaching to complete them all at an optimal level. Instead of seeking to maximize your performance in all tasks, be picky about the tasks you give most of your effort to.

Few things are as spiritually demoralizing as doing work that you believe in with students who emphatically do NOT share your beliefs. The good news is that student beliefs are malleable and that we as teachers can, over time, make a significant impact on those beliefs.
Teaching is beautiful work, colleague, but it's also so very hard sometimes.
